title: Much (of), many (of), a lot of, lots (of), etc.
subtitle: a lot of traffic / much debate
summary: Pick the right quantifier for the context: a lot of and lots of in conversation, much (of) and many (of) in formal writing, and the fixed patterns in between.

lesson.heading: Conversation or formal writing?

left.label: a lot of, lots (of) - affirmative and informal
examples: There's bound to be **a lot of / lots of** traffic on the way to the station.
**A lot of / Lots of** people think that hedgehogs are very rare nowadays.
... but when I was in Wales I saw **a lot / lots**.

right.label: much (of), many (of) - formal, e.g. academic writing
examples: **Much** debate has been heard about Thornton's new book.
There could be **many** explanations for this.
**Much of** her fiction describes women in unhappy marriages.
**A large amount of** the food was inedible. (or **Much of** ...)
The book contains **a large number of** pictures, **many** in colour.

lesson.note: Formal alternatives: a large / considerable / substantial amount of (uncountable nouns); a large / considerable / great / substantial number of (plural nouns).

lesson.heading: much and many as pronouns
lesson.text: In formal contexts we can use **much** and **many** on their own, with no noun after them.

examples.text: There is no guarantee she will recover. **Much** depends on how well she responds to treatment.
**Many** have argued that she is the finest poet of our generation.
Not once did I see a tiger in the jungle, although I heard **many**.

lesson.heading: many with times and numbers
lesson.text: We usually use **many** rather than *a lot of* or *lots of* with time expressions (days, minutes, months, weeks, years) and with *number + of*.

examples.text: We used to spend **many hours** driving to Melbourne and back.
He was the founder of a company now worth **many millions** of pounds.

lesson.heading: the / my / its many, and many a
lesson.text: **Many** can follow *the, my, its, his, her*, etc. with a plural countable noun. **Many a** with a singular noun talks about a repeated event or a large number of people or things.

examples.text: Among **the many** unknowns after the earthquake is the extent of damage to the foundations of buildings.
The gallery is exhibiting some of **his many** famous paintings of ships.
**Many a** pupil at the school will be pleased that Latin is no longer compulsory.

lesson.heading: a good / great many, a good / great deal of
lesson.text: To emphasise a large **number** we use **a good / great many** with a plural noun. To emphasise a large **amount** we use **a good / great deal of** with a singular or uncountable noun. The two are not interchangeable.

examples.text: She has **a good / great many** friends in New Zealand.
**A good / great deal of** the exhibition was devoted to her recent work.

lesson.heading: far too many, far too much
lesson.text: We use **far** - not *much* or *many* - before **too many** + a plural countable noun and **too much** + an uncountable noun.

examples.text: **Far too many** students failed the end-of-year maths exam.
**Far too much** time is wasted filling in forms.

lesson.heading: plenty of means enough
lesson.text: We often use **plenty of** instead of *a lot of* or *lots of* with uncountable and plural countable nouns. But *plenty of* means *enough, or more than enough*, so it is unlikely where the amount is unwelcome.

examples.text: We took **lots of / plenty of** food and drink on our walk through the hills.
Nina doesn't look well. She's lost **a lot of** weight.

lesson.text: Two quick tests: *much / many* sound formal in an affirmative sentence, so save them for writing; and *plenty of* only fits when having that much is good news.

exercises.prompt: In conversation: 'Lola's had ___ problems with her back.'
exercises.explanation: In informal, affirmative sentences a lot of is more usual than many.

exercises.prompt: Lola's had a lot of problems with her back for ___ years.
exercises.explanation: With time expressions such as years, hours and months we usually prefer many.

exercises.statement: A lot of people think that hedgehogs are very rare nowadays, but when I was in Wales I saw a lot.
exercises.explanation: Correct. In conversation a lot of and the pronoun a lot (or lots) are more usual than many.

exercises.prompt: A: There's bound to be a lot of traffic on the way to the station. B: No, there's ___ time left.
exercises.explanation: The quantifier is plenty of - the of cannot be left out.

exercises.prompt: Can the gap be filled with plenty of, or does it need a lot of?

items.text: It will be very hot on the journey, so make sure you bring ___ drinking water.
I'm looking forward to a relaxing holiday, and I'm taking ___ books to read.
___ staff at the hospital have come down with a mysterious illness.
He didn't have ___ money, so he decided to catch the bus rather than take a taxi.
We were surprised when ___ students failed to attend the lecture.
Nina doesn't look well. She's lost ___ weight.

exercises.prompt: In academic writing: '___ have claimed that Professor Dowman's study on current attitudes to politics is flawed.'
exercises.explanation: In formal writing many can stand alone as a pronoun meaning many people.

exercises.prompt: Put the words in order to make one sentence.
exercises.answer: Far too much time is wasted filling in forms.
exercises.explanation: Before too much and too many we use far, never much or many.

exercises.prompt: In academic writing: '___ research has been conducted on the effects of diet on health.'
exercises.explanation: much (of) and many (of) are preferred in formal contexts such as academic writing.

exercises.prompt: The area is most famous for ___ that attract players from all over the world.
exercises.explanation: many can follow the, my, its, his or her before a plural countable noun.

exercises.prompt: ___ has been lost in the dangerous waters off the south coast of the island.
exercises.explanation: many a + singular noun refers to a repeated event or a large number of things.

exercises.prompt: She's having an operation next week and she won't be back at work for ___ weeks afterwards.
exercises.explanation: a good / great many goes with a plural noun; a good deal of cannot.

exercises.prompt: In addition, ___ hi-tech companies have moved in to take advantage of the newly available workforce.
exercises.explanation: companies is a plural noun, so a great deal of is impossible - a great many is needed.
